Maju Forest, Gillman Barracks: Fewer homes and more greenery retained in revised housing plans
article:
HDB has revised the conceptual plans for the proposed housing developments at the Maju Forest and Gillman Barrack sites to allocate more land for greenery and reduce the development footprints by about 1,200 homes.

This follows environmental studies for both sites, a heritage study for Gillman Barracks, and feedback from the public and stakeholders.

In total, both sites are expected to yield around 11,000 homes over the next decade, HDB said on Oct 28.

This comprises roughly 4,000 public housing units at Maju Forest at Sunset Way, and some 7,000 homes at Gillman Barracks. The latter includes about 5,500 HDB flats.

That works out to a reduction of 400 flats at Maju Forest and 800 units at Gillman Barracks as compared to the original plans.

These are estimates based on broad planning assumptions and will need to be further studied at the detailed design stage, HDB noted.

Now that more land will be set aside for greenery, HDB said it also intends to efficiently use the remaining development area to provide new homes, such as by building taller blocks.

More details, such as the housing mix and launch dates, will be shared when ready.

Meanwhile, about 10ha, or 45%, of the Maju Forest site will be retained as greenery. That is up from around 8ha, or 35%, initially.

"The additional retained green area at the southern part of the site will result in a wider and more contiguous green area that will strengthen ecological connectivity within the site and along the Clementi Nature Corridor," said HDB.

And at Gillman Barracks, the area set aside for greenery will increase from 8ha, or 40% of the existing greenery in the area, to about 12ha, or 60%.

More of the existing forest around the hillock will be retained, which will provide a greener frontage towards Telok Blangah Street 31. The north-south ecological corridor along Lock Road and Malan Road will also be widened.

"These refinements will enhance the ecological connectivity within the Southern Ridges, as well as towards Berlayar Creek and Labrador Nature Reserve," HDB said.

The National Parks Board (NParks) will also safeguard a "significant portion" of the greenery at both sites as nature parks, to enhance nature conservation, the housing authority added.

In reviewing the housing plans for both sites, government agencies weighed the ecological importance of retaining more greenery against housing needs and other land use considerations, given the circumstances of each site.

The public consultation period ran from July 10 to Aug 6, during which HDB received about 7,200 feedback submissions for Maju Forest and 2,300 for Gillman Barracks.

In addition, about a thousand stakeholders — including nature groups, youths, academics, planning and built-environment professionals — were engaged. Local grassroots advisers also spoke with residents living near both sites.

The initial announcement of the proposed housing developments on July 10 had caused a stir, with months of vigorous debate about issues including environmental conservation, ecology, climate resilience, heritage, housing demand, alternative sites, as well as the planning process and public participation.

Petitions calling for the protections of the sites reportedly attracted more than 50,000 signatures in total.

title: Thomson Reserve collects around 3,200 cheques ahead of Oct 31 launch
article:
Thomson Reserve , the largest new private residential launch of 2026 with 1,268 units, has collected around 3,200 cheques ahead of its sales launch on Oct 31, signalling strong buying interest in the 99-year leasehold development at Bright Hill Drive, off Upper Thomson Road.

The cheque collection represents a subscription rate of over 2.5 times. VIP bookings will begin on Friday, Oct 30, ahead of the official launch on Saturday.

The strong response follows a preview turnout of 11,800 visitors over the opening weekend of Oct 17 and 18, and more than 23,000 visitors in the first week.

For joint developers UOL Group , its subsidiary Singapore Land Group (SingLand) and CapitaLand Development (CLD) , the response raises expectations of another successful launch, following ParkTown Residence in February 2025 and Skye at Holland in October that year.

Both 99-year leasehold developments attracted substantial cheque collections ahead of their launches and went on to achieve take-up rates of 87% to 99% over their respective launch weekends.

Kelvin Fong, CEO of PropNex, believes pricing will be key to sustaining sales momentum at Thomson Reserve. “For Thomson Reserve, which has over 1,200 units, we expect developers to keep prices attractive enough to build sales momentum, especially during the initial stages of the launch,” he says.

From cheque collection to sales

ParkTown Residence, part of a mixed-use development integrated with a transport hub in Tampines North, collected 2,367 cheques for its 1,193 units ahead of its launch, representing a subscription rate of about two times.

The project went on to sell 1,041 units, or 87% of the development, over its launch weekend in February 2025, at an average price of $2,360 psf. That translated to a cheque-to-sale conversion rate of 44%.

ParkTown Residence was 98% sold as at Oct 27, with an average transacted price of around $2,356 psf, based on caveats lodged.

Eight months later, the 666-unit Skye at Holland in prime District 10 collected 2,151 cheques ahead of its October 2025 launch, representing a subscription rate of 3.2 times.

Of these, 658 converted into purchases, for a conversion rate of 30.6%. The development nearly sold out over its launch weekend, with 99% of units sold at an average price of $2,953 psf.

The project was fully sold as at May 1, when the last 1,765 sq ft, five-bedroom suite found a buyer at $5.85 million ($3,316 psf), based on a caveat lodged.

For Thomson Reserve, the 3,200 cheques collected have already surpassed the numbers recorded at both earlier projects. However, its subscription rate remains below that of Skye at Holland, given its larger size of 1,268 units, nearly double Skye's 666 units.

"UOL and CLD have demonstrated their ability to identify sites with strong locational attributes and enhance their appeal through thoughtful project development, as seen at ParkTown Residence and Skye at Holland," says Mark Yip, CEO of Huttons Asia.

He adds that the developers are in tune with market conditions and tend to price their projects competitively, “leaving something on the table for buyers”.

Yip believes Thomson Reserve could replicate the success of their earlier launches, given its elevated 5ha site, proximity to popular schools and doorstep access to Upper Thomson MRT Station. “Buyers are not just buying a unit at Thomson Reserve, but buying into the entire 5ha development,” he adds.

Unit mix and buyer appeal

Thomson Reserve comprises two residential collections. The Classic Collection has 740 units across four 21-storey towers, while the Luxury Collection comprises 528 units in two 30-storey towers.

The Classic Collection offers two- to four-bedroom layouts, while the Luxury Collection features two-bedroom premium units to five-bedroom suites. Of the 528 units in the Luxury Collection, 112 larger four-bedroom premium units and five-bedroom suites feature private lift access.

Two-bedroom apartments account for 716 units (56.5%), with sizes ranging from 592 to 775 sq ft and prices starting from $1.544 million ($2,608 psf). Another 350 units (27.6%) are three-bedroom apartments, with prices starting from $2.503 million. Together, these two unit types make up 84% of the development.

Four-bedroom apartments account for 174 units (13.7%), with prices starting from $3.388 million ($2,737 psf).

The 28 five-bedroom suites, each measuring 1,808 sq ft, occupy a single stack with unblocked views towards MacRitchie Reservoir and the Orchard Road skyline. They account for just 2.2% of the development.

Units overlooking the surrounding nature reserves and reservoir are said to be particularly sought after. Prospective buyers also include those looking to live close to their parents in the Upper Thomson and Bishan neighbourhoods.

Another draw is the proximity to popular schools. Ai Tong School is less than 1km away, while CHIJ St Nicholas Girls' School (Primary) and Catholic High School (Primary) are within 2km.

The development is also a two-minute walk from Upper Thomson MRT Station on the Thomson-East Coast Line, with easy access to Thomson Plaza , eateries along Upper Thomson Road and the surrounding nature reserves.

Thomson Reserve occupies the former Thomson View Condominium site, which the developers agreed to acquire in a collective sale in November 2024 for $810 million. The price translates to $1,178 psf per plot ratio, including the estimated cost of topping up the lease to a fresh 99 years and land betterment charges.

“Interest in Thomson Reserve has been strong across the board for all unit types,” says Marcus Chu, CEO of ERA Singapore. “The indicative prices are reasonable and attractive.”

Beyond Thomson Reserve, the UOL-CLD joint venture has secured two other major development sites in Hougang Central and New Upper Changi Road , opposite Bedok Mall, which are expected to yield a combined 1,840 residential units.

Chu believes the developers will be focused on achieving healthy sales at Thomson Reserve this weekend, given their substantial pipeline of upcoming residential projects.

“The developer will likely price Thomson Reserve this weekend with a focus on recycling inventory and capital, given that they already have a healthy and strong pipeline of future sites,” he adds.

title: Freehold ground-floor retail unit on Lorong Kilat in Beauty World for sale at $8.5 mil
article:
A first-floor strata retail unit at Sun Court , a residential development on Lorong Kilat in the Beauty World area, is up for sale through an expression of interest (EOI) exercise. The freehold unit has a guide price of $8.5 million, or $3,495 psf on its strata area of 2,432 sq ft.

The unit is approved for restaurant use and is currently tenanted, according to marketing agent Huttons Asia. “At approximately 2,432 sq ft, this freehold ground-floor unit offers the scale that many operators look for when planning a more substantial dining concept,” added Yeo Khee Liang, associate senior marketing director at Huttons.

Sun Court is a freehold apartment block at 21 Lorong Kilat with retail units on the ground floor. Completed in 1985, it has less than 20 residences. It is part of a row of similar low-rise developments on Lorong Kilat, about a five-minute walk away from the Beauty World MRT Station on the Downtown line.

Retail shops at the developments serve the surrounding Beauty World and Bukit Timah residential enclaves, included the nearby landed housing estates off Jalan Jurong Kechil and Upper Bukit Timah Road .

“Retail spaces in Lorong Kilat are seldom put up for sale,” said Lee Sze Teck, senior director of data analytics at Huttons.

Lodged caveats show just one transaction for a Lorong Kilat commercial unit in the past five years. A freehold strata shop at Sun Court changed hands for $2.05 million in June 2021, which works out to $1,380 psf on its 1,485 sq ft strata area.

The EOI will close at 3pm on Nov 24.

The per-unit numbers do.

Can CICT keep its DPU growth ahead of growth in its unit base?
CICT is Singapore’s largest REIT by market capitalisation.
It owns retail, office and integrated development properties, with total assets of S$28.2 billion as at 30 June 2026.
For the first half of 2026 (1H2026), gross revenue rose 7.5% year on year (YoY) to S$846.8 million, while net property income (NPI) climbed 8.7% to S$630.5 million.

Here’s the thing: CICT’s unit base grew 5.8%, and yet DPU still came out ahead.
Portfolio occupancy rose 0.4 percentage points quarter on quarter to 95.6%.
Retail occupancy hit 97.7%, above the Urban Redevelopment Authority’s (URA) islandwide figure of 93.5%.
Rental reversions stayed positive at 4.0% for retail and 6.5% for office.
So what’s new this time? Paragon.
CICT completed the S$3.9 billion acquisition on 1 July 2026, just after the half ended, so watch for its first contribution.
The sale of Asia Square Tower 2, for net proceeds of about S$2.45 billion, is expected to be completed in 2H2026.
Aggregate leverage improved to 37.4% as at 30 June 2026, and average cost of debt held steady at 2.9% – though both figures precede Paragon’s completion.

In 1H2026, gross revenue rose 6.7% YoY to S$805.5 million, and NPI grew 6.2% to S$556.1 million.

However, DPU rose by just 0.1% YoY to S$0.07482.
Why the gap?
Equity fundraisings in 1H2025 and 1H2026 lifted the number of units entitled to distributions by 8.5%, and the new units absorbed most of the income growth.
To put it simply, CLAR earned more, but each unit’s share barely moved.
Occupancy slipped to 89.1% from 91.8% a year ago.
For context, part of the decline reflects the addition of two newly completed properties.
Excluding them, occupancy would have been 90.3%.
Rental reversions came in at 8.5% for 1H2026, and management expects them to stay positive in the high single digits for the full year.
CLAR has also announced a further S$638.1 million in acquisitions and plans to divest Kim Chuan Telecommunications Complex for S$200.4 million, representing a 32% premium to its valuation.
Aggregate leverage stood at 39.7%, the highest of the three REITs, with cost of debt at 3.5%.

Its latest figures cover just one quarter, the first quarter of the fiscal year ending 31 March 2027 (1QFY2027).

VivoCity remains the bright spot.

Portfolio committed occupancy fell to 84.4% from 89.3%. Japan, at 56.0%, and China, at 82.4%, dragged the figure lower.
Rental reversions came in at −9.1% for Festival Walk and −29.2% for China.
The absence of income from divested assets and a stronger Singapore dollar also weighed on the quarter.
That leaves the payout leaning on VivoCity and lower finance costs.
A recovery in overseas NPI would put it on firmer ground.
Watch Festival Walk’s 18,800-square-foot reconfiguration, which became operational in July 2026.
MPACT puts its return on investment at close to 50%, though on a small outlay of about HK$5.3 million.
Aggregate leverage stood at 37.7%, and cost of debt improved to 2.94%.

title: Is Venture Corporation’s Cash-Rich Dividend Payout Plan Sustainable?

A company can pay out more than it earns for a while, but for how long?
Venture Corporation Limited
(SGX: V03) is an established Singapore electronics manufacturer.
The company has paid a
dividend
every year since its listing in 1992.
Now, where is the dividend coming from: the earnings or its balance-sheet cash?
Let’s find out.

Venture has paid at least S$0.75 per share every year since FY2020.
That includes FY2023, when net profit fell about 27% year on year (YoY).
In FY2025, the dividend went up to S$0.80 thanks to a one-off
special dividend
of S$0.05 paid alongside the interim dividend.
At current prices, Venture offers a trailing annualised yield of about 5.3%.
The company’s latest interim dividend stood at S$0.30 per share, unchanged from FY2025.
Now, there is no fixed dividend payout policy; instead, management says it is committed to enhancing shareholder returns.
How Strong Is Venture’s Cash Position?
As at 30 June 2026 (1H2026), Venture had net cash of S$1.11 billion (zero debt), making up roughly 25% of its market capitalisation.
Cash grew from S$807.9 million at end-FY2021 to S$1.28 billion at end-FY2025.
At a dividend per share of S$0.80, it costs Venture roughly S$230 million a year to keep its stable payout.
That works out to roughly 4.8 years of payments given its current net cash position.
But cash on the balance sheet is flexibility, not a promise.
A manufacturer requires cash to fund its working capital and to also support growth investments.
Can Venture’s Earnings Support Its Dividends?
Earnings are recovering slowly; revenue rose 7.4% YoY to S$1.35 billion, and net profit increased 5.6% to S$119.3 million.
Consequently, earnings per share (EPS) came in at S$0.414, up from S$0.392.
The mix matters: in 2Q2026, networking, test and measurement, and chip equipment customers lifted revenue by 25.7%, offsetting an 8.5% decline in life science, MedTech and consumer products.
Crucially, net margin eased to 8.8% (1H2025: 9.0%).
As seen in the table, Venture’s payout ratio was 101% in FY2025, meaning it paid out slightly more than it earned.
Worryingly, this also continues the trend over the last few years of increasing payout ratios.
That is fine for a year or so, but not indefinitely.
What happens if the company maintains its payout but earnings decline?
A 10% decline in EPS would push the payout ratio to 113% and leave a S$26 million yearly gap between earnings and dividends.
A 20% decline would push the payout ratio to 127% and leave an annual shortfall of S$49 million.
A short dip is easy to survive.
A long slump is different.
The cash would last, but it would shrink each year, and the board would face a choice between a cut and a smaller safety net.

A high yield can mean investors expect a cut, and a 99% payout of the past 12 months’ earnings gives them a reason to.
The valuation doesn’t show that fear.
Venture trades at 18.6x its earnings over the past 12 months.
That sits between DBS’s 16.7x and Singtel’s 20.7x.
Its P/B ratio is 1.6x, against 3.0x for DBS and 2.6x for Singtel, though a bank and a telco hold very different assets.
Strip out the S$3.86 a share of net cash and the business trades at about 14 times earnings.
On FY2022’s peak earnings of S$1.27 a share, today’s price would be just 12x.
So the price already factors in the cash and some recovery.
It isn’t a bargain.
The dividend case strengthens if earnings per share climb back near S$1.00, which would bring the payout to about 80%.

The warning signs are a payout above 100% for a second year, net cash under S$1 billion and another year of weak cash flow.

The dividend is sustainable for the next few years, but only because of the cash.
Net cash covers about five years of payments, and even a 20% drop in earnings would leave a manageable gap.
It is not yet self-funded.
The payout ratio was 101% in FY2025 and about 99% over the past 12 months, and FCF covered just 0.4 times the past year’s dividends.
A recovery in customer orders could change that, and 1H2026 growth is a good start.
If it stalls, the cash pile is the only thing holding the S$0.80 up.

It’s tempting to reach for the biggest payouts on offer.
A lower share price does nothing to protect a dividend, though.
Cash does.
So before you buy, ask how a company pays for what it hands you.
The three SGX companies below all

Can Union Gas keep paying more as it adds stations?
Union Gas Holdings Limited
(SGX: 1F2) distributes gas fuels and runs Cnergy service stations.
Its profit attributable to shareholders rose 175.8% year on year (YoY) to S$12 million.
The board could have lifted the regular dividend to match.
It didn’t; instead, it held the interim dividend steady and paid a special dividend instead:
Interim dividend: S$0.0048 per share, unchanged from a year ago
Special dividend: S$0.0032 per share, the group’s first
Total dividends rose 66.7% YoY to S$0.008 per share.
All of that increase came from the special, so don’t count on it every year.
The cash backs it up.
Free cash flow climbed to S$25.1 million, up from just S$1.3 million a year ago, helping the group maintain a healthy net cash position of S$21.7 million as at 30 June 2026.
The growth was largely driven by its service station network, where total revenue rose 66.4% to S$105.9 million.
Liquid fuel revenue jumped 444.4% to S$51.7 million as new stations at Dunman Road and Queensway began contributing.
Growth won’t come free.
Stations in Marsiling and Jurong West are due to open in 2027, and the group spent S$8.2 million buying two LPG retailers on 31 July 2026.

Forget the Blue Chips: 4 SGX Stocks Quietly Outperforming the STI
3 SGX Hidden Gems Surprising Investors with Bonus Dividends
Is Nanofilm’s bigger dividend backed by lasting cash flow?
Nanofilm Technologies International Limited
(SGX: MZH) makes advanced materials coatings and nanofabricated products.
It doubled its interim dividend to S$0.006 per share on the back of a 65.6% YoY surge in net profit to S$4.3 million.
While that percentage jump looks impressive, it comes off a relatively small base from the prior period.
Cash flow told a bigger story.
Free cash flow turned positive at S$19.5 million, up from an outflow of S$10.3 million from the previous year.
Free cash flow is the lifeblood of dividends, and here it ran far ahead of profit.
Part of that gap came from customers paying what they already owed, but don’t expect that boost every half.
Revenue grew 6.1% to S$113.7 million, but the more lasting change shows up in margins.
Gross margin widened to 38.6% from 32.6% as automation and cost discipline lifted productivity.
Research and engineering expenses also rose 56.6%.
Much of that reflects accounting, not extra spending: as projects moved into production, less of the cost was set aside to be expensed in later years.
Total R&D spending actually fell to S$17.4 million from S$19.1 million.
Cash of S$88.7 million roughly matched total bank borrowings of S$88.8 million as at 30 June 2026.
The second half of the year will test the recovery.
Management expects stronger equipment deliveries in 2H2026, helped by its order backlog.
Conversely, tighter memory chip supply and rising component prices may squeeze margins.
Related articles:
Beyond Blue Chips: 3 SGX Stocks Quietly Buying Back Their Own Shares
Top 3 Small-Cap Stocks Big Money Is Buying in April 2026
What does ValueMax’s borrowing mean for its dividend?
ValueMax Group Limited
(SGX: T6I) runs pawnbroking and secured moneylending businesses, and retails and trades gold and jewellery.
It raised its interim dividend 15% YoY to S$0.0138 per share, which was paid out on 3 September 2026.
Net profit attributable to shareholders increased 30.4% to S$62.6 million, giving the dividend hike plenty of cover relative to earnings growth.
Revenue rose 38.2% to S$370.7 million, though gross margin narrowed to 27.0% from 30.2% as lower-margin gold sales made up more of the mix.
Here’s the thing: ValueMax lends money for a living, so its cash flow looks different.
Free cash flow came in at negative S$34.1 million, compared to negative S$14.5 million a year earlier, as trade and other receivables absorbed S$192.7 million to fund loan book expansion.
For a financial lender, growing the loan book builds future earnings power, but it naturally consumes cash upfront.
That growth leans on borrowing.
Total borrowings, excluding lease liabilities, reached S$1.05 billion as at 30 June 2026, up 18.1% over six months, against cash and bank balances of S$18.8 million.
That debt is why ValueMax is the most nuanced case of the three.
Management expects gold prices to stay volatile after peaking near US$5,300 an ounce in March 2026, and it has flagged rising competition.
Get Smart: Trace the cash before you buy the dip
A
falling share price
tells you nothing about whether a payout will last.
So follow the money.
Start by separating any special dividend from the ordinary payout, as Union Gas shows.
Then ask whether free cash flow came from the business or from collecting old receivables.
Nanofilm’s latest half had a bit of both.
And at ValueMax, borrowing pays for growth, so keep an eye on that debt.

Just make sure you pick the ones whose cash you understand.

title: Should You Sell Your Losers When the Market Dips?
article:
Last week, Citi downgraded
Oversea-Chinese Banking Corporation
(SGX: O39), or OCBC, to “sell”.
The reaction was swift.
By the end of last week (9 October), shares of OCBC and
United Overseas Bank
(SGX: U11), or UOB, were around 11 per cent below their 52-week highs.
Meanwhile,
DBS Group
(SGX: D05) was down by a little over seven per cent.
In turn, the
Straits Times Index
(SGX: ^STI) was around 7.3 per cent off its peak.
While the decline was quick, it’s not a
market correction
— that would be a decline of 10 per cent or more.
Yet, the mood has shifted just as quickly.
A week ago, I reckon many Singapore bank shareholders were wondering how much higher their shares could go.
Now, they’re wondering how far their shares could fall.
Here’s the truth: the banks’ operations haven’t changed in a week.
So why does a modest dip feel so unsettling?
When the pain of loss overwhelms the joy of gains
Imagine this: you open your brokerage account and see two stocks.
One is sitting on a S$1,000 paper gain.
The other is sitting on a S$1,000 paper loss.
In theory, there is no difference between the two.
The gain cancels out the loss, and your portfolio hasn’t moved a single cent.
In practice, there is. The joy of gains is often overwhelmed by the dread of losses.
Which one will your eyes keep going back to? I bet it’s the loser.
It’s not just you. It’s how we are wired.
Psychologists Daniel Kahneman and Amos Tversky called this loss aversion: losses loom larger than gains of the same size.
In “Thinking, Fast and Slow”, Kahneman notes that losses typically weigh 1.5 to 2.5 times as much as equivalent gains.
That’s why last week’s dip may have felt far bigger than seven per cent.
Here’s the thing: loss aversion didn’t start working last week.
It was there all along, even when stocks were rising.
It simply asks a different question about our losers, depending on which way the market is moving.
Are you scared or embarrassed?
When share prices fall, risks move to the forefront.
Risks which were already present become the centre of discussion.
When prices rise, the focus changes.
Your losers aren’t collapsing.
They simply aren’t keeping up — it’s the few red figures that stick out like a sore thumb in a sea of green.
So, you ask: why isn’t my stock keeping up?
Therein lies the danger.
Fear
is loud.
As last week showed, you know when you are feeling it.
Embarrassment is quiet.
It doesn’t feel like an emotion at all.
Instead, it feels like an opportunity loss — your money isn’t working as hard as it should.
In my view, that makes it the more dangerous of the two.
It quietly nudges you to sell your losers and put the money into the stocks that have done really well.
It looks like discipline.
But more often than not, it’s the pain of loss looking for an exit.
Yet, few investors who make this swap would call it embarrassment.
Most would call it opportunity cost.
The seductive logic of opportunity cost
The idea behind opportunity cost is simple.
Every dollar stuck in a lagging stock is a dollar that isn’t compounding in a winning stock.
To be fair, these investors aren’t wrong about the concept.
But an accurate concept does not guarantee an accurate execution.
There’s nothing wrong with the intention.
Most of us want our portfolios to squeeze out every bit of return.
The trouble starts when optimising becomes the driving force behind every decision.
More often than not, that urge comes from the nagging sense that you are falling behind.
And an investor who feels behind is prone to mistakes: trading too often, chasing stocks that have already run, and giving up on good businesses too soon.
Here’s the paradox: if you want better returns, stop optimising for returns.
Optimise for your peace of mind instead.
A sound mind makes better decisions.
And better decisions, compounded over years, lead to better performance.
Economist John Kay calls this obliquity: some goals are best reached indirectly.
Get Smart: Ask a better question
So, what should you do the next time a red number catches your eye?
Start by changing the question.
“Why have shares fallen?” is about the scoreboard.
The better question works in any market — is the business performing the way it should?
Take
the banks
.
Nothing has changed in the financial figures they reported in early August.
The share price moves since then, up or down, have been driven by sentiment.
To answer the question, revisit why you bought the stock.
If you keep an investing journal, check the reasons you wrote down and the risks you flagged.
Then try the fresh-cash test: would you buy this stock today, at today’s price?
If the answer is no because the business has deteriorated significantly, sell — whether the number is red or green.
But if it is yes, the red number is just noise.
Remember the two stocks at the start?
In theory, they’re the same. In practice, they never will be.
You can’t switch off loss aversion.
But you can stop letting it ask the questions.
Your losers may embarrass you.
Just don’t let them make your decisions.

title: Mercedes readies major China overhaul as slump deepens
article:
(Oct 28): Mercedes-Benz Group AG is preparing a broader overhaul of its China strategy after the luxury-car market deteriorated more sharply than expected, insisting it has no plans to retreat from what remains the world’s largest auto market.

Chief executive officer Ola Källenius said conditions in China are “deteriorating beyond what we had thought would happen this year”, with weakness intensifying further in the second half. The downturn has been particularly severe at the upper end of the market, where Mercedes has traditionally held a strong position and generated some of its richest margins.

Källenius said Mercedes is reviewing everything from its product line-up to sales, production, sourcing and technology in China, with a broader strategy to be presented in 2027.

“There is not a play where you put China aside,” he told analysts on Wednesday. “It has to be one of the pillars of your strategy.”

The reassessment comes as Mercedes pushes ahead with its biggest product and cost overhaul in years. Third-quarter revenue fell 4.5% to €30.7 billion (US$34.1 billion or $43.8 billion), while adjusted group earnings before interest and tax declined 15%, the German carmaker said on Wednesday. A day earlier, Mercedes lowered its outlook, citing a worsening China slump and higher costs.

At the core cars division, adjusted earnings more than halved to €560 million in the third quarter, and the margin narrowed to 2.5% from 4.8%, reflecting the weaker contribution from China as well as currency and product-launch costs.

See also: Pop Mart's 3Q sales fall up to 50% as Labubu fad cools

Mercedes vehicle sales in China fell 31% in the third quarter from a year earlier, extending a decline driven by weaker luxury demand, fierce price competition and increasingly sophisticated domestic rivals.

Mercedes shares fell less than 1% on Wednesday in Frankfurt, following Tuesday’s 3.9% decline. The stock has lost more than a third of its value this year.

See also: China’s 5-year government bond yield trades near record low

Källenius said Mercedes isn’t treating the decline as a reason to downgrade China to a niche market. Beyond its sheer size, the country remains important because of its fast-moving technology ecosystem and the growing global reach of Chinese suppliers and automakers, he said.

The company is instead trying to remake the economics of selling cars there. A coming electric E-Class was developed from what Källenius described as effectively a “white sheet of paper”, with a product tailored more closely to Chinese buyers and sourcing shifted much more heavily into the country.

Mercedes will get close to sourcing the vehicle entirely in China for local production, Källenius said, helping cut variable costs significantly compared with its previous model. The company also plans to price the car realistically for local market conditions rather than relying on the economics that underpinned its China business in the past.

Still, Källenius ruled out chasing volume at any cost. Mercedes won’t adopt the “fire sale market-share-at-all-cost” approach pursued by some competitors, he said, underscoring the tension between protecting the brand and competing in one of the world’s fiercest price wars.

Chief financial officer Harald Wilhelm said the company expects its new-model momentum to strengthen further in 2027, alongside continued reductions in variable costs. But he declined to predict where China will be by then, saying the company would give a clearer assessment when it reports full-year results in February.

The comments add to signs that Mercedes increasingly sees China as a structural challenge rather than a temporary cyclical downturn. For years, CEO Ola Källenius has pursued a strategy centered on selling fewer but more expensive cars, relying heavily on models such as the S-Class, Maybach, G-Class and AMG range to support margins.

That calculation has become harder as China’s property downturn weighs on luxury spending and local rivals challenge Mercedes on price, software, electric technology and increasingly design.

Mercedes is responding with both cost cuts and its largest-ever product offensive. More than 40 new or refreshed models are due by the end of 2027. The electric CLA and GLC are already being rolled out, with new versions of the C-Class, S-Class, GLE and GLS among the vehicles intended to revive demand.

The company is also targeting material-cost savings of around 8% compared with 2024 levels, with substantially deeper reductions planned in China, and is shrinking an industrial footprint built for stronger volumes. Voluntary redundancy programmes are being used to reduce the German workforce.

The pressure extends across Germany’s auto industry. BMW AG and Volkswagen AG have also warned that deteriorating conditions in China are hurting earnings, highlighting how quickly a market that once generated outsized profits has become one of the sector’s biggest structural problems.

Volvo Car AB CEO Håkan Samuelsson said last week that the market for Western-developed cars in China isn’t coming back.

title: Malaysian billionaires said to revive plan to create nation’s biggest mobile operator
article:
(Oct 28): The Malaysian billionaire families behind Maxis Bhd and U Mobile Sdn Bhd are reviving plans to combine the companies in a deal that could create the country’s biggest wireless operator by market value, people with knowledge of the matter said.

Maxis, backed by the holding company of late tycoon T Ananda Krishnan, is moving a step closer to a merger by asking a select group of banks and law firms to submit proposals, the people said. The company could pick advisers shortly, according to the people, who asked not to be identified because the information is private.

The potential transaction is gaining traction as both sides are showing more willingness to negotiate, the people said. Shares of Maxis have fallen around 5% this year, giving the company a market value of about RM28.3 billion ($8.9 billion).

U Mobile’s owners may seek a valuation of RM10 billion or more in a deal, some of the people said. A combination of the two companies would overtake CelcomDigi Bhd, which has a market capitalisation of about RM29 billion, as the country’s biggest mobile operator.

Closely held U Mobile is controlled by a vehicle backed by Malaysian princess Tun Aminah Sultan Ibrahim Ismail — the daughter of the country’s billionaire King — and businessman Tan Sri Vincent Tan.

See also: Intel said to buy quantum start-up Classiq for about US$2.3 bil

The two firms have had on-and-off discussions on a merger for several years. Maxis had considered buying out U Mobile and had early discussions on the matter in 2024, Bloomberg News reported at the time. Local weekly The Edge Malaysia reported earlier this year that talks between the two parties had stalled because the parties couldn’t agree on valuations.

U Mobile was picked by the Malaysian Communications and Multimedia Commission in 2024 to implement the country’s second 5G network. It completed the migration to its own 5G network in July.

Tun Aminah’s father, Sultan Ibrahim Sultan Iskandar, is the hereditary ruler of Malaysia’s southernmost state of Johor. He took the throne in 2024 for a five-year term as the King of Malaysia under the country’s rotating monarchy system.

See also: EQT to buy Range Resources, creating largest US gas producer

Mawar Setia Sdn Bhd, a company controlled by the princess and Tan, owns more than 50% of U Mobile. Singapore Technologies Telemedia Pte Ltd, a unit of Singapore state investment firm Temasek Holdings Pte Ltd, cut its shareholding to 20% after agreeing to sell part of its stake to Mawar Setia.

Deliberations are ongoing and there’s no certainty they will reach an agreement, the people said. A spokesperson for Maxis said the company “is always evaluating strategic opportunities and partnerships that are value-accretive” and will disclose any material developments.

A representative of the late Krishnan’s private investment vehicle, Usaha Tegas Sdn Bhd, declined to comment. Tan also declined to comment. Spokespeople for U Mobile and ST Telemedia didn’t respond to queries.

title: Hong Lai Huat sets up investment subsidiary in Singapore, eyes real estate opportunities
article:
Mainboard-listed Hong Lai Huat Group has incorporated Huat Assets Management, a new wholly owned subsidiary in Singapore. The subsidiary will identify and pursue investment opportunities across various real estate sectors in Singapore, according to an Oct 28 bourse filing.

The incorporation forms part of the group’s ongoing efforts to explore suitable real estate investment opportunities in Singapore, according to Hong Lai Huat.

With the aim of generating recurring rental income and achieving long-term capital appreciation, Huat Assets Management’s investment activities “may include property acquisitions, asset management, strategic divestments, asset enhancement and redevelopment opportunities, where commercially viable”.

The group is currently evaluating suitable investment opportunities in Singapore.

The property developer currently holds two completed projects in Cambodia: D’Seaview, which has 737 residential units and 67 commercial units. Royal Platinum, which is a joint venture, has 851 residential units and 50 commercial units.

The company has previously been involved in various boutique condominium projects across Singapore’s eastern region. Speaking to The Edge Singapore in June, Hong Lai Huat executive director and chief strategy officer Dylan Ong said the group will be looking at potential land banks in Singapore for boutique residential development.

See also: Hong Lai Huat maintains property focus despite marble mining bonanza in Cambodia

Shares in Hong Lai Hut closed 3.5% higher at 6 cents on Oct 28, down some 25% year to date.

title: Adani flagship returns to profit as newer businesses deliver
article:
(Oct 28): Billionaire Gautam Adani-controlled Adani Enterprises Ltd returned to profit in the second quarter as newer businesses including airports and data centres scaled up.

Net income was 14.9 billion rupees for the three months ended Sept 30, according to an exchange filing on Wednesday. While that is 55% lower than the year-ago profit, the performance marks a return to black after the company had reported a loss of 11.6 billion rupees in the previous quarter amid costs linked to settlement of US legal cases.

Revenue climbed 75% year-on-year to 372.2 billion rupees and costs rose 71% to 360.2 billion rupees, the filing showed. Shares of the Adani Group flagship slipped 0.4% after the earnings were announced, in line with the fall in the S&P BSE Sensex.

The return to profitability could ease investor concerns about funding requirements for expansion and that newer businesses are approaching an earnings inflection point. Airports, data centres, roads and clean-energy ventures are expected to play a growing role in Adani Enterprises’ profit mix as they start generating cash flow.

Revenue from the integrated resources management — a unit that mostly consists of coal trading and contributes the most to the company’s overall revenue — rose 6.6% to 70.97 billion rupees. The airports business is surging in the mix, with its revenue rising 15% to nearly 37 billion rupees. New energy and commercial mining units also posted rising revenue from year-ago period.

See also: Chinese EV imports surge in Thailand ahead of planned excise tax

Gross debt for Adani Enterprises slipped 0.3% from the preceding quarter to 972.94 billion rupees.

In May, the US Department of Justice dropped criminal bribery charges against Gautam Adani and his nephew, Sagar Adani, after they agreed to pay US$18 million to settle a parallel civil fraud case there.

See also: Universal Music discussed going private with buyout firms

The ports-to-power conglomerate accelerated its growth plans after resolving its legal troubles in the US. In May, the Department of Justice dropped criminal bribery charges against Adani and his nephew, Sagar Adani, after they agreed to pay US$18 million to settle a parallel civil fraud case there. Separately, Adani Enterprises paid US$275 million to resolve a sanctions probe by the Office of Foreign Assets Control. Neither the executives nor the company admitted wrongdoing.

Drawing a line under its US regulatory probes stoked a 43% rally for the stock earlier this year but the shares have tumbled more than 20% from their peak in July, wiping out almost US$10 billion in market value.

The growth prospects for its airport and copper businesses, as well as its joint venture with Jabil for artificial intelligence and data centre equipment manufacturing will stay in focus for investors in the coming months, with consensus expectations for the stock to rally more than 40% in the next 12 months.

title: Asia leads US-friendly nations in cutting their purchases of Treasury by 60%
article:
(Oct 28): Being one of Washington’s closest partners no longer means reliably funding the US deficit.

Countries and regions most aligned with the US bought a net US$174.3 billion of Treasuries, excluding bills, in the first eight months of 2026, according to an analysis of Treasury and State Department data. That was the lowest for the period since 2021 and down more than 60% from a year earlier.

The shift is noteworthy in Asia, where economies running large surpluses are putting less of that money into US debt. Japan, the biggest foreign holder of Treasuries, bought just US$389 million in the first eight months — down 99% from a year earlier. South Korea sold US$23.8 billion, the most for the period in records going back to 1977. Taiwan was also a net seller.

There’s no single explanation for the shift. Governments have said little about any plans to move away from Treasuries, and the data don’t separate government buying from private investment at the country level. Several factors may be contributing, including weak currencies, rising yields at home, growing demand for stocks and unease over US policy.

“The Treasury market isn’t losing foreign buyers — it’s losing automatic buyers,” said Masahiko Loo, a senior fixed-income strategist at State Street Investment Management, which oversees over US$6 trillion. “An increasingly unpredictable US makes large structural overweights and the automatic recycling of capital into Treasuries harder to justify.”

See also: AI tech fears push global credit spreads to 17-month high

The US government’s debt pile has climbed past US$40 trillion, leaving the world’s largest economy more reliant on investors to fund its spending. At the same time, President Donald Trump’s tariffs and uncertainty over US policy have spurred concerns about the dollar’s longer-term outlook. And with yields rising in markets from Japan to Europe, global investors have more alternatives to Treasuries than they once did.

Asia’s big savers have typically converted their surpluses into dollars and parked the money in Treasuries. This year, weakening currencies eroded their buying power and pushed governments to dip into reserves.

The yen sank to its weakest level in four decades, and data suggested Tokyo sold some of its Treasuries and other securities over the summer as it sought to support the currency. The won fell to its lowest since 2009 before recovering.

See also: Paris unrest poses contamination risks to bond yields beyond France

Governments haven’t shed much light on their approach. In May, a senior Japanese Finance Ministry official suggested that selling Treasuries to prop up the yen is counterproductive, saying authorities are mindful of the risks of selling their holdings. The Bank of Korea said in September it plans to broaden investments beyond US bonds for a portion of its reserves managed by domestic asset managers.

Alignment can be subjective. This analysis, an update of one first published in February, classifies countries as most-, least- and neutrally-aligned by how often their votes on key United Nations resolutions match those of the US, using State Department data. The approach is commonly used in academia to determine allies and adversaries.

For example, longtime military ally Australia was classified as most-aligned, China as least, with America’s neighbour Mexico falling into the neutral bucket.

The figures are net purchases — buying minus selling — of Treasuries with an original maturity of more than one year. They cover 57 countries and regions and include both official and private investors.

The Treasury data may attribute securities to the country where they are held through custodians or intermediaries, rather than to the nation of the ultimate owner. Holdings and purchases attributed to financial centers such as the UK and Belgium may therefore partly reflect investors elsewhere.
